We examined the learning rate (the unstandardized regression coefficient indicating the strength of the relationship between the estimation error and the subsequent update) for good and bad news for the self and a friend using repeated measures analyses of variance, controlling for the differences in estimation errors between good and bad news for both conditions (see https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129. 2).
For Study 2b, we preregistered the hypothesis, sampling procedures, and analysis plan (https://osf.io/a5bmw/).
We report the preregistered analyses in the https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129 which produced the same results as reported here.

Because the predicted interaction between valence and identifiability was only at trend level, we conducted a preregistered replication study using a larger sample on the basis of the effect size found in Study 2a (https://osf.io/a5bmw/).
As in Study 2b, we preregistered our hypothesis, methods, participant recruitment strategy, and analysis before running the studies and analyzing the data (osf.io/zmf4c).

In a pilot study, another set of participants (N = 40) rated both strangers (liked and disliked) on likability (likability, generosity, warmth, blameworthiness, morality, friendliness; see the https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129 for factor analyses confirming one general-likability dimension) as well as intelligence and health.

The learning bias for the self condition and the learning bias for the stranger condition were not significantly correlated, r(76) = .10, p = .386 (see https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129. S3b in the https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129).

Individual differences in the magnitude of vicarious optimism for strangers were positively correlated with donations to charity, r(76) = .26, p = .02 (see https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129. S4b in the https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129). This relationship was robust to controlling for the magnitude of the optimistic learning bias for self, age, gender, education, and income, partial r(70) = .29, p = .012 (see the https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/suppl/10.1177/0956797617737129 for details).
